# Continental drift and plate tectonics (`plate_tectonics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs deep_time_geology; helped by world_geography, terrestrial_magnetism
- Core idea: The Earth's outer shell is broken into a dozen rigid plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow, carried by slow flow in the hot rock beneath. Where plates part, new sea floor forms along mid-ocean ridges; where plates converge, one may sink beneath another, forming trenches and volcanic arcs, or two continents may collide and build mountains. Plates also slide past one another along faults. Evidence available early: the coasts of South America and Africa fit, and the same rock formations, fossils and traces of ancient ice continue across the join. Earthquakes and volcanoes lie in narrow belts along plate edges, which tells where they must be expected.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying continents plough through the ocean floor (Wegener's weak point); the sea floor moves with them
  - Expecting acceptance on the coastline fit alone; geologists rejected drift until sea-floor evidence in the 1960s
  - Claiming earthquakes can be predicted to the day
  - Giving speeds of metres per year
- History: europe: 1596 Ortelius notes the fit of the Atlantic coasts; 1912–1915 Wegener, continental drift; 1929–1931 Holmes proposes mantle convection; 1963 Vine and Matthews, magnetic stripes; americas: 1962 Hess, sea-floor spreading; 1965–1968 Wilson, Morgan and others formulate plate tectonics; africa: 1937 – du Toit (South Africa) assembles the southern-continent evidence
- Read:
  - Alfred Wegener, Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane (1915)
  - Naomi Oreskes, The Rejection of Continental Drift (1999)
